topic: mending a torn drift net: cutting back to whole meshes, twine weight and a stretched belly

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: echosonda zapisujaca glebokosci

base: I tore a long rent in my drift net on a rock and want to mend it properly.
An old herring net hangs in the loft and its mending patches have held for years.
The echo sounder in the wheelhouse writes down every depth we tow across.
The rent runs eleven meshes along one side and about four meshes across.
Should I cut the whole piece out, or work the needle straight into the torn edge?
Cut the piece out first, because a torn edge has half meshes that will never match.
Trim back to whole meshes on all four sides and count them before you start.
A mend begun on a ragged edge pulls crooked and the net hangs badly forever after.
Use twine of the same weight as the net, never heavier, whatever the shop suggests.
I cut back to whole meshes and now have a clean hole of nine by four.
The twine on the reel matches the net for weight, though it looks a shade paler.
The old herring net was mended with tarred twine, which has darkened almost to black.
Does the colour matter to the fish, or only to the man doing the work?
Colour matters little at the depths you work, since light is nearly gone by then.
Tar mattered more, because it kept hemp from rotting through a season of use.
Your synthetic twine needs no tar, so the pale patch is nothing to worry about.
Start at a corner mesh, work across in rows and keep the knots all facing one way.
I worked across in rows and the patch came out square with even meshes throughout.
We towed the net twice this week over the ground where the rock lies.
The echo sounder logged nine fathoms there, a good fathom less than the chart says.
Should I keep clear of that ground, or shorten the warp and tow shallower?
Keep clear of it, because a rock that takes one net will take another.
Charts of inshore ground are old and a fathom of error is entirely ordinary.
Mark the spot in your own notebook and give it fifty yards of clearance.
Shortening the warp changes how the net fishes and rarely helps on hard ground.
I marked the rock in the notebook and we have towed clear of it since.
The mended patch has held through six hauls without a single mesh giving way.
The net now sags a little in the belly, more than it did before the tear.
Is the patch pulling it out of shape, or has the whole net stretched?
The whole net has stretched, which every net does over its first two seasons.
A patch of nine meshes cannot pull a belly out of shape on its own.
Check the belly against the wings and see whether the sag runs right across.
If it does, take the stretch up at the headline rather than cutting the belly.
The sag ran right across, so I took the stretch up along the headline.
The net fishes better now and the catch has improved on the same ground.
The old herring net in the loft has never stretched at all, as far as I can tell.
Was hemp really steadier than the twine we buy today, or is that just talk?
Hemp stretched less, that part is true, but it rotted and had to be barked each year.
A hemp net lasted perhaps four seasons where yours will last ten with care.
The loft net kept its shape partly because it stopped fishing many years ago.
Judge your own net after another season, once the stretch has finally settled down.
